report.source_text: On arrival, her blood pressure was 150/80, her blood glucose level was 101 mg/dL, her heart rate was in the 70s (beats per minute), and there was active AF with a right bundle branch block on electrocardiogram. She reported no pain she was afebrile. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) was 1 for mild dysarthria; no motor deficits or weakness was appreciated on her initial examination. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15, fully alert and oriented. Her pupils were equal and reactive on both sides. Modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score was 1.

The heparin drip was restarted immediately after the procedure.

clinician.trajectory_summary: 83-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped rivaroxaban the morning before presentation due to planned cataract surgery. She presented at 04:30 with acute onset nausea, dysarthria, left-sided tingling, and difficulty speaking. Initial neurological examination showed minimal deficits (NIHSS 1 for mild dysarthria only, no motor weakness, GCS 15, equal reactive pupils). Vital signs were BP 150/80, HR 70s, glucose 101, afebrile. ECG showed active AF with right bundle branch block. Non-contrast CT head was normal, ruling out hemorrhage. CT angiogram of the head and neck revealed distal basilar artery occlusion with right superior cerebellar artery perfusion deficit. Mechanical thrombectomy was performed within one hour of symptom onset without acute complications. Post-thrombectomy CTA showed widely patent basilar artery with no residual distal embolus. The next morning, patient was near baseline with no neurological deficits but reported mild dizziness and vivid visual hallucinations (which she recognized as unreal). Repeat head CT was negative for intracranial bleed. Heparin drip was restarted immediately after thrombectomy. Patient was discharged after a few days in stable condition with long-term stroke risk reduction plan including rivaroxaban and high-intensity statin therapy.
